title: Fusing two derangement recurrences with the CRT
content: The parent entry proves two separate divisibility facts for the derangement numbers D(n) = numDerangements n: (A) (n−1) ∣ D(n) for n ≥ 2, from the additive recurrence D(n) = (n−1)(D(n−1)+D(n−2)); and (B) n ∣ (D(n) − (−1)^n), from the multiplicative recurrence D(n) = n·D(n−1) + (−1)^n. The open question asks whether these can be combined into a single congruence modulo n(n−1). Because consecutive integers n and n−1 are coprime, the Chinese Remainder Theorem fuses (A) and (B) into one statement, and the crucial observation is that a single closed form (−1)^n·(n−1)² satisfies both residue conditions simultaneously for every parity.

title: Fact (A): (n−1) divides D(n)
content: The additive recurrence numDerangements_add_two states D(m+2) = (m+1)·(D(m+1) + D(m)). Writing n = m+2 exhibits (n−1) = (m+1) as an explicit factor, so (n−1) ∣ D(n) for n ≥ 2. The proof obtains the witness ⟨D(m) + D(m+1), …⟩ and discharges the equation with simpa over the Mathlib recurrence — no arithmetic beyond unfolding the recurrence is needed.

title: Fact (B): n divides D(n) − (−1)^n
content: The multiplicative recurrence numDerangements_succ gives D(k+1) = (k+1)·D(k) + (−1)^(k+1), so D(k+1) − (−1)^(k+1) = (k+1)·D(k) is divisible by k+1. Cast to ℤ so the alternating sign (−1)^n is available, then push_cast and ring close the goal after supplying the witness D(k). The n = 0 case is handled separately by simp.

title: Consecutive integers are coprime
content: The CRT fusion relies on gcd(n, n−1) = 1. Over ℤ this is witnessed by the explicit Bézout identity 1·n + (−1)·(n−1) = 1, so IsCoprime holds by ⟨1, −1, by ring⟩. Working with IsCoprime (rather than Nat.Coprime) is deliberate: it feeds directly into IsCoprime.mul_dvd, the abstract CRT combiner used in the main theorem, and it lives over ℤ where the signed residue (−1)^n(n−1)² is expressed.

title: (n−1)-component of the residue
content: Half of the CRT combination: (n−1) divides D(n) − (−1)^n(n−1)². The term (−1)^n(n−1)² is divisible by (n−1) because (n−1)² is (dvd_pow_self then mul_left), and D(n) is divisible by (n−1) via Fact (A) for n ≥ 2. The small cases n = 0, 1 are dispatched by interval_cases with direct evaluation. Subtracting the two divisibilities (dvd_sub) yields the claim.

title: n-component of the residue
content: The other half: n divides D(n) − (−1)^n(n−1)². Rewrite the target as the sum (D(n) − (−1)^n) + (−1)^n(1 − (n−1)²). Fact (B) handles the first summand; the second is divisible by n because 1 − (n−1)² = n(2 − n), giving the explicit witness ⟨2 − n, by ring⟩. Adding the two divisibilities and rewriting back with ring completes the component.

title: Main result: the combined modulus n(n−1)
content: The theorem mul_dvd_sub_crt assembles the two component divisibilities through IsCoprime.mul_dvd: if coprime a, b each divide x, then a·b divides x. Here a = n, b = n−1, x = D(n) − (−1)^n(n−1)², giving n(n−1) ∣ x — i.e. D(n) ≡ (−1)^n(n−1)² (mod n(n−1)), the full CRT combination the open question sought. The entire proof is a single term applying mul_dvd to the two component lemmas.

title: ZMod restatement of the congruence
content: The divisibility is repackaged as an equation in the quotient ring ℤ/n(n−1)ℤ: D(n) = (−1)^n·(n−1)² in ZMod (n(n−1)). The bridge is ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd, which turns 'the modulus divides an integer' into 'that integer is zero mod the modulus'; a cast lemma matches the integer product n(n−1) with the natural-number modulus, and linear_combination finishes. This form makes the result usable directly in modular computations.

title: The canonical reduced residue r(n)
content: The closed form (−1)^n(n−1)² is not the canonical representative for odd n (it is negative). Reducing mod n(n−1) gives r(n) = (n−1)² when n is even and r(n) = (n−1) when n is odd. This definition captures the smallest non-negative residue of D(n) modulo the combined modulus, packaged as a parity branch on Even n.

title: r(n) lies in the fundamental domain
content: For n ≥ 2 the reduced residue satisfies 0 ≤ r(n) < n(n−1), so it is the unique canonical representative. Both branches follow from the single bound 1 ≤ n−1: positivity handles non-negativity, and nlinarith proves the upper bounds (n−1)² < n(n−1) and (n−1) < n(n−1). The strict inequality is what pins r(n) down as THE representative rather than merely A representative.

title: Canonical congruence D(n) ≡ r(n)
content: First closedForm_sub_reduced_dvd shows the closed form and the reduced residue agree mod n(n−1): for even n they are literally equal (Even.neg_one_pow collapses the sign), and for odd n the difference −(n−1)² − (n−1) = −(n−1)·n is a visible multiple. Adding this to the main result (numDerangements_sub_reduced_dvd) transfers the congruence from the signed closed form to the canonical residue: D(n) ≡ r(n) (mod n(n−1)). This is the sharpest form of the answer.

title: Concrete sanity checks
content: Worked instances confirm the formulas by decide: D(5) = 44 with modulus 20 and signed closed form (−1)^5·16 = −16, so 44 − (−16) = 60 = 3·20; D(6) = 265 with reduced residue 5² = 25, so 265 − 25 = 240 = 8·30; and r(5) = 4 (odd branch), r(6) = 25 (even branch). These make the abstract congruence tangible and guard against off-by-one or parity errors.
